text.en: Gurpreet plays with his fraction kit. He fits one half piece and two fourth pieces together to make a whole. What is the link between one half and two fourths?

Two fractions that show the same part of a whole, but have different names, are called equivalent fractions.
One half is equivalent to two fourths. When one half piece is broken into 2 equal parts, each part is one fourth, so 2 pieces of one fourth are equal to one half.
Sameer shaded one-third of a figure. He drew lines to cut it into more equal parts and saw 1/3 = 2/6 = 3/9 = 4/12. The shaded region did not change, only the name did.
The pattern: multiply the top number and the bottom number by the same number to get an equivalent fraction. 1/3 x 2/2 gives 2/6, and 1/3 x 3/3 gives 3/9.
In the same way 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 = 4/8, and 1/4 = 2/8 = 3/12.
You can use the kit to make a whole from different pieces, for example half, fourth and fourth, or 1/6 and 1/12 pieces, or 1/12, 1/4 and 1/2 pieces.
Equivalent fractions are a way to show that a fraction has many names for the same amount.
In the book a shaded strip shows that 1/3 and 2/6 name the same part of a whole. These are called equivalent fractions, as the same part of a whole can have different names.
Sameer shades one-third of a figure and draws horizontal lines to divide it into more equal parts. The shaded part is 1/3, then 2/6, then 3/9 and then 4/12, all the same shaded region. So 1/3 = 2/6 = 3/9 = 4/12.
Look for the pattern: for 1/3 the next fractions are 2/6, 3/9, 4/12, then 8/24 and 12/36. The top and bottom numbers are multiplied by the same number each time (see the diagram).
The same is shown for 2/5: it equals 4/10, which equals 20/50 and 40/100. Fill in the boxes to make fractions equivalent, such as 2/5 = ?/10 or 3/4 = ?/16, and tick the pairs that are equivalent.
